stem: Which of these is an indigenous beef breed of Zimbabwe?

options.content: Mashona
options.rationale: Correct: a hardy, fertile Sanga breed.

options.content: Hereford
options.rationale: An exotic British breed.

options.content: Brahman
options.rationale: An exotic zebu breed developed in the USA.

options.content: Simmental
options.rationale: An exotic Swiss breed.

explanation: Indigenous breeds include the Mashona, Nkone and Tuli.

stem: Which beef breed has a red body and a white face?

options.content: Hereford
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Tuli
options.rationale: The Tuli is yellow to golden-brown.

options.content: Brahman
options.rationale: The Brahman is usually grey or red with a large hump.

options.content: Mashona
options.rationale: Mashona cattle vary in colour, often black or red, without a white face pattern.

explanation: The Hereford is an early-maturing British breed with a white face.

stem: Which feature makes the Brahman well suited to hot, tick-infested areas?

options.content: A thick, woolly coat
options.rationale: A thick coat would make heat stress worse.

options.content: Loose skin and many sweat glands that help it lose heat
options.rationale: Correct: zebu cattle tolerate heat and resist ticks well.

options.content: A white face that reflects sunlight
options.rationale: That describes the Hereford, which is less heat tolerant.

options.content: Very short legs and a small body that needs only a little feed every day
options.rationale: The Brahman is a large breed.

explanation: Brahmans have loose skin, a large dewlap and good sweating ability, and are used to add heat and tick tolerance in crosses.

stem: Why do beef cattle on veld often receive a protein or urea lick in the dry season?

options.content: Licks stop the cattle from drinking too much water
options.rationale: This is not their purpose.

options.content: Protein licks kill ticks on the skin
options.rationale: Ticks are controlled by dipping.

options.content: Dry grass contains too much protein, which the lick neutralises
options.rationale: Dry grass contains too little protein.

options.content: Dry grass is low in protein, so cattle lose mass
options.rationale: Correct: the lick feeds rumen microbes so more fibre is digested.

explanation: Protein and urea licks correct the protein shortage of dry veld grass and help cattle hold their condition.
hints: What is dry-season grass short of?

stem: Cattle on a ranch are seen chewing old bones, and some have died of botulism. Which supplement should the rancher provide?

options.content: A urea lick only
options.rationale: Urea supplies nitrogen for protein, not phosphorus.

options.content: Extra water
options.rationale: Water does not correct the deficiency.

options.content: A phosphate lick
options.rationale: Correct: bone chewing is a sign of phosphorus deficiency.

options.content: Maize grain mixed with molasses to give them more energy for grazing
options.rationale: Energy feeds do not correct phosphorus shortage.

explanation: Phosphorus-deficient cattle chew bones and may pick up botulism toxin; phosphate licks (and vaccination) prevent it.
hints: What does a phosphorus-deficient animal do?

stem: What is the main advantage of a controlled breeding season in a beef herd?

options.content: Cows produce two calves a year
options.rationale: Cows still have at most one calf a year.

options.content: Calves are of similar age and can be managed and sold as a group
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: Bulls can be sold because they are not needed
options.rationale: Bulls are still needed during the breeding season.

options.content: Calves are all born in the dry season when the veld grass is short and dry
options.rationale: The season is timed so calves come near the start of the rains.

explanation: A short calving season gives uniform calves for branding, dosing, weaning and sale, and matches feed needs to the grazing.
hints: Think about managing calves as a group.

stem: Why are steers introduced to a high-grain pen-fattening ration gradually over about two weeks?

options.content: Because grain is too expensive to feed in large amounts at first
options.rationale: Cost is not the reason for the gradual start.

options.content: So the steers lose weight first and then gain it back
options.rationale: The aim is steady gain.

options.content: Because cattle cannot taste grain until they have eaten it for two weeks
options.rationale: This is not true.

options.content: To let the rumen microbes adjust and avoid bloat and an over-acid rumen
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: A sudden change to grain causes rapid fermentation, acid build-up and bloat; a gradual change lets the microbes adapt.
hints: What happens in the rumen if a lot of grain is eaten suddenly?

stem: Branding cattle with the owner's brand helps to prove ownership and deter stock theft.
explanation: True. Brands are permanent marks of ownership; ear tags identify individuals for records.

stem: Indigenous breeds such as the Mashona usually grow faster than exotic breeds such as the Simmental when both are well fed.
explanation: False. Exotic breeds grow faster with good feeding; indigenous breeds are hardier and survive drought, ticks and poor grazing better.

stem: Match each management practice with its main purpose.

right.content: Prevents unwanted mating and gives docile steers
Prevents horns and the injuries they cause
Lets the cow regain condition before the next calf

explanation: Each routine practice has a clear reason.

payload.template: The {{blank:a}} is an indigenous breed developed in Zimbabwe, yellow to golden-brown in colour, while the Brahman is an exotic {{blank:b}} breed with a large hump.

explanation: Tuli; the Brahman is a zebu (Bos indicus).

stem: Assume a ratio of one bull to 25 cows. How many bulls are needed for 175 cows?
A steer grew from 320 kg to 446 kg in 90 days in a feedlot. Calculate its average daily gain in kg/day.
A steer weighing 420 kg live produced a carcass of 243.6 kg. Calculate the dressing percentage.
explanation: 243.6 ÷ 420 × 100 = 58%. Dividing live mass by carcass mass gives over 100%, which is impossible.

stem: Explain why indigenous cattle such as the Mashona are well suited to communal areas in natural regions IV and V.

points.description: They are hardy and survive on poor, dry veld with little supplementary feed.
They tolerate heat and resist ticks and tick-borne diseases better than exotic breeds.
They are fertile and good mothers, producing calves regularly even in poor conditions.
They survive droughts and recover condition quickly / are also used for draught.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Mashona cattle are hardy and live on poor dry veld, tolerate heat and resist ticks, keep calving regularly as fertile, good mothers, and recover quickly after drought, so they suit dry communal areas.

explanation: Adaptation to feed, climate, disease and fertility.
hints: Give a breed, then a feature and why it helps.

stem: A feedlot near Chinhoyi fattened 20 steers for 110 days. Their mean mass was 280 kg on entry and 412 kg at sale, and the group ate 21,120 kg of ration.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the average daily gain of a steer, in kg/day.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the feed conversion ratio of the group.
parts.explanation: Total gain = 20 × 132 = 2,640 kg; FCR = 21,120 ÷ 2,640 = 8. Using one steer's gain gives 160, which forgets there are 20 steers.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Total gain = 20 × 132 = 2,640 kg; FCR = 21,120 ÷ 2,640 = 8. Using one steer's gain gives 160, which forgets there are 20 steers.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** things done to the steers when they arrive at the feedlot.

points.description: Dosed against worms and dipped/sprayed against ticks.
Vaccinated / weighed and identified / introduced gradually to the grain ration.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of pen fattening compared with finishing the steers on veld.

points.description: Advantage: faster gain and a higher slaughter grade in a short time / relieves dry-season grazing pressure.
Disadvantage: high cost of feed, pens and labour; risk of bloat/acidosis.

explanation: Calculate feedlot performance and evaluate pen fattening.

stem:
The number of calves born each month on two beef farms in one year.

| Month | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Farm X | 3 | 4 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 2 | 2 |
| Farm Y | 0 | 0 | 14 | 18 | 10 | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which farm runs its bulls with the cows only during a short breeding season?

options.content: Farm X
options.rationale: Farm X has calves in every month, so its bulls run with the cows all year.

options.content: Both farms
options.rationale: Farm X's calving is spread through the year.

options.content: Farm Y
options.rationale: Correct: its calves are born within about four months.

options.content: Neither farm, because both have calves in December
options.rationale: Farm Y's calves are concentrated in October to January.

parts.explanation: Farm Y's calving is concentrated from October to January.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of Farm Y's calves born in October and November, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why Farm Y times its calving for October to December.

points.description: Calves are born near the start of the rains.
So the cows have new, green grazing when they need most feed for milk, and calves grow well.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain **three** management advantages Farm Y gains from its calving pattern.

points.description: Calves are of similar age, so branding, dosing, vaccination and weaning are done in groups.
Calving can be supervised in a short period, reducing losses.
Weaners are uniform and sold together; cows that did not calve are easily identified and culled.

explanation: Interpret calving patterns and explain the value of a breeding season.
hints: Which farm uses a breeding season?
Percentage = calves in October and November ÷ all calves × 100.
